speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was encouraging to read that the new Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Mulroney) recognizes that Canada has become a country of regions and has long since ceased to be a simplistic community of communities.
Permit me to quote my own words of March 10, 1981, on this matter:
This nation, Canada, will increasingly evolve, and its interdependence will increasingly grow as a co-operative quasi economic and social federation of five national regions. Within these regions, Provinces shall co-operate and compete, shall integrate transportation and energy and other systems and shall evolve somewhat different and unique social and cultural systems. And over all, all these regions shall form the umbrella of a reorganized national Parliament.
The relationship of the national umbrella and the regional well-being, aspirations and growth will be dynamic, changing and challenging. This then is, and will continue to be, the essence of Canada.
The patriation of the Constitution and the entrenchment of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was a giant leap, and a mandatory one, toward this vision of Canada. Structural reform of the Senate on the basis of the five regions of Canada is also mandatory. Our nation shall endure and prosper.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. What is the position of the Government of Canada in regard to the reported Marxist takeover in Grenada which was accomplished by murdering the Prime Minister, a number of his colleagues, and leading trade unionists on the island?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: GRENADA-MURDER OF PRIME MINISTER IN MARXIST TAKEOVER-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the events in Grenada have been very unfortunate. That type of violence cannot be condoned.
Oral Questions
The Government has made a statement, which I actually made earlier this morning, to express our distress as a Government at the events, as well as my own personal sorrow because, although Maurice Bishop had an ideology which is not ours, he was in the Commonwealth and engaged in dialogue with us. 1 dare say he was a friend. Therefore I am very sorry at the turn of events.
We have expressed our dismay. 1 believe the Minister of State may have further up to date details, but this was my response as of earlier this morning.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Mulroney (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we share the thrust of the Prime Minister's statement of regret, of course, but in view of the brutality and murder involved, does this impact in any way on the thinking of the Government in regard to aid programs directed to that particular country in which, in this situation, the beneficiaries would become people, as the Prime Minister has indicated, with whom he would not like to do business?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I doubt whether that has been envisaged in the Department yet. I would only indulge in a bit of hindsight here.
This Government had given some modest assistance to Grenada. We did it in spite of cries-some of which I am afraid came from the other side-to the effect that that Government was left leaning. It is now apparent that there are more left leaners than Maurice Bishop was, and that it is wise not to cut off relations with Governments with which we may disagree if they are following policies which seem correct to them in their particular part of the world.
In other words, I have never been an advocate of cutting off countries because I disagreed with their ideology. I believe, and I have previously stated this precisely about the Grenada case, that when a country tries to export its revolution, then we indeed should show very great displeasure and take action. But I do not think we should try to influence the choice of independent peoples by using our aid programs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nor do I hold the view that one must necessarily reflect the political philosophy of the donor nation so as to benefit from foreign aid-not by a long shot.

My understanding of the authority of the House to proceed as it choosed is contained in Citation 13 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition where the following words may be found at page 6 under the heading "Unanimous Consent". Citation 13 reads:
13. (1) Within the ambit of its own rules, The House itself may proceed as it chooses; it is a common practice for the House to ignore its own rules by unanimous consent. Thus, bills may be passed through all their stages in one day, or the House may decide to alter its normal order of business or its adjournment hour as it sees fit.
(2)	The House is perfectly able to give consent to set aside its Standing Orders and to give its unanimous consent to waive procedural requirements and precedents concerning notice and things of that sort.
As authority, the Debates for June 28, 1977, at page 7154, are cited.
If, as practice and Beauchesne indicate, it is within the authority of the House to waive its rules through unanimous consent, it follows that Members have the right to seek unanimous consent to waive procedural requirements and precedents. The only means by which a Member can seek unanimous consent is to ask, through the Chair, for the consent of the House to waive the ordinary rules.
I submit that the Chair is bound to seek unanimous consent when that consent is sought by any Hon. Member. Citation
411	of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition describes the process of debate. Citation 411(1) reads as follows:
Every matter is determined in the House of Commons upon a question put by the Speaker, on a proposition submitted by a Member, and resolved either in the affirmative or negative as the case may be. This proposition, called a motion, is a proposal moved by one Member, in accordance with certain well-established rules, that the House do something or order something to be done or express an opinion with regard to some matter.
As Citation 411(1) clearly states, every matter is determined in the House of Commons upon a question put by the Speaker on a proposition submitted by a Member. Citation
412	considers the definition of a question. It states at page 150:
The question is the subject matter of the motion, and on the merits of that subject matter the House has to give a decision either unanimously or by the majority of the members present. Every question when agreed to assumes the form either of an order or a resolution of the House. By its orders the House
October 20, 1983

directs its committees, its members, its officers, the order of its own proceedings and the acts of all persons they concern; by its resolutions the House declares its own opinions and purposes.
(2) When a motion is adopted, it becomes the resolution or order of the House. Therefore, its form must consequently be so framed, and its language so expressed that, if it meets the approbation of the House, it may at once become the resolution or order of the House which it purports to be.
On the basis of the citations to which I have referred, Madam Speaker, it would seem that the House may, by unanimous consent, set aside its usual rules and practices and that within that authority the House may consider motions that could not otherwise be moved. Because unanimous consent may be granted to set aside rules that would otherwise block a motion from being moved, the seeking of unanimous consent from being moved, the seeking of unanimous consent cannot be said to be out of order, in my submission.
As well, the seeking of unanimous consent to move a motion is a separate proposition submitted by a Member to the Speaker who must, according to the ordinary practices of the House, put the question, that is: Is there or is there not unanimous consent? The question, in this case, requires the unanimous decision of the House and should meet the other requirements set forth in Citation 412, such that if it is agreed to it may at once become the resolution of the House that it purports to be.
In this case, the question, the seeking of unanimous consent, if agreed to becomes a resolution of the House to permit the Member to move his or her motion. Thus, the motion is completely regular within the terms of Citation 412.
The next issue that has to be considered, Madam Speaker, is whether or not the House business question is the appropriate occasion for Members to rise on points of order to seek unanimous consent to move motions dealing with business that is now, or will soon be, before the House. I can think of no more appropriate time to seek the consent of the House to move a motion that would facilitate the business of the House than during the House business question. Indeed, this is a practice often followed by the House Leaders for all Parties in the House. Citation 158 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition refers to the House business question in the following manner in paragraph 4, found at page 50:
(4) As a matter of practice, since 1968, each Thursday following the Question Period, the Government House Leader states, in reply to a question put by the House Leader of the Official Opposition, the projected business of the House for the forthcoming week.
The practice with respect to the House business question has evolved somewhat further since the Fifth Edition of Beauchesne's was published. Points of order are justified when there is some flagrant misuse of the rules, but they are unfortunate necessities which should not be regarded as usual phases of procedure and ought not to develop into long arguments with the Speaker who, being in a quasi-judicial position, should not be drawn into controversial discussions.

(2) A Member cannot rise on a point of order to move a motion.

AIR CANADA-GIMLI ACCIDENT-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO SAFETY PROCEDURES. (B) DISCIPLINING OF EMPLOYEES-REQUEST FOR POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) is in the House. I am sure he will want to stay long enough to respond to my
concerns about the Gimli accident. We are going to discuss a glider plane known as a 767. Captain Robert Pearson and First Officer Morris Quintal probably saved the Canadian taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars by safely landing that aircraft at Gimli, Manitoba, not to mention the 69 lives aboard that plane.
It appears very likely to me as a Member of Parliament that the President of Air Canada, Claude Taylor, has, with the assistance of the Minister of Transport, committed a blatant cover-up of the Gimli accident by having a behind closed doors hearing-not one but two-on this accident and then trying to cover up, intentionally or otherwise, the information given at those two hearings. We have conflicting information. First we have a statement on October 6 in The Toronto Sun reporting the Minister of Transport as saying:
Meanwhile, Transport Minister Lloyd Axworthy rejected demands for a public inquiry into the controversial landing.
Then we go to the Air Canada report. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that that report was brought in by seven members of a commission, five of whom were employees of the Boeing Company, manufacturer of the aircraft in question. If that does not indicate a direct conflict of interest, then I do not know what would. However, after a couple of behind closed doors investigations, we then had the statement, as reported in The Globe and Mail on September 30, by Mr. Taylor, the President of Air Canada, who said on September 29:
-the report shows that Air Canada's operations are "still of the highest order.
It is reassuring to know from recognized independent experts that the series of incidents during 1983 do not reflect a deterioration in Air Canada's technical and operating proficiency."
Mr. Taylor also said:
At the outset it should be clarified that the independent audit was initiated by Air Canada-
He goes on to say:
-as to whether there were any fundamental or substantive flaws in our technical and operating procedures.
I am pleased to state that the audit team confirmed that these were still of the highest standard.
Having reviewed his comments, I would like to move now to the comments of the Chairman of that Commission. These comments will give an entirely different picture. First, as reported in the Montreal Gazette on October 18:
The checks of the Edmonton-bound jet with 69 people aboard at Montreal and Ottawa failed to discover a malfunctioning fuel-indicating system and the problem was further compounded by a failure to convert from metric volume to metric weight, the report says.
The accident investigation report concludes the maintenance and flight crews acted "in contravention of the Minimum Equipment List", and transport officials in Canada and the United States agree that would mean the aircraft was not airworthy.
If we go one step further in this report which was never released to the public, we find that he told The Gazette that the 767 pilot had never received any training in the refueling procedures for the 767. According to this accident report which has never been made public:
October 20, 1983

-the flight crew maintain the calculations made by them were to cross check figures provided by maintenance" while the maintenance technician "insists that he did not .. . supply the flight crew with fuel figures in kilograms."
Remember that these are the only flights in Canada, North America and the world, except Russia, that use the metric system. The report says that this was the first time they were asked to perform a drip check manual measurement of fuel on the Boeing 767 and had not received any formal training on the procedure.
My concern is that if they have not received any training as ground crew or technicians, why are the pilot and co-pilot reprimanded, demoted or dismissed for an error that was caused by the lack of procedural guidelines laid out by Air Canada?
Let us proceed to Mr. Robert Buck, who is the Chairman of the Commission that investigated this accident. He said, "You cannot have a bastard group of metric planes flying in an Imperial fleet." He also said that this special behind closed door hearing never reviewed the Gimli accident. We have the President of Air Canada saying "We are 100 per cent safe", and the Chairman of the Commission appointed by the President of Air Canada saying, "We never even discussed the Gimli accident", and "You cannot have bastard planes flying around."
The Minister has left the House since I started to speak and does not wish to respond as Minister responsible. He has now determined that we need a public inquiry. There is one county court judge from Gimli, Manitoba, who will be able to call witnesses. I wonder if he will call Mr. Buck? I wonder if he will call the Air Line Pilots Association of Canada? I wonder if he will call in the air traffic controllers?
1 am only concerned that we are getting another ramrod job by the Minister of Transport trying to whitewash, using a pilot and co-pilot as scapegoats to take the fall for the errors of Air Canada.

TRUST COMPANIES-REFUSAL TO REWRITE MORTGAGES AT LOWER RATES. (B) PROTECTION REQUESTED FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 28, as reported at page 27534 of Hansard, I raised a question in the House with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) regarding the plight of approximately 750,000 Canadians who have mortgages with high interest rates. This matter has been raised a number of times in the House. In fact, it goes back as far as April, 1980, when the Government, in its Throne Speech starting this Session of Parliament, mentioned the difficulty being faced by home owners in securing mortgages for their homes. Many times since then, Ministers have expressed concern and indicated they would do something about the difficulty in which 750,000 Canadians find themselves.
Briefly, the situation is as follows. Mortgages have been acquired by a large number of people from a handful of trust companies on the clear understanding that they could prepay the mortgages upon the payment of a three-month interest penalty. We have established in writing that three months interest penalty was a standard policy in the industry. When the home owners tried to prepay their mortgages they were told that the policy had been changed, and it was now required that an interest differential charge be paid in addition to the three-month interest penalty.
This move by the trust companies was clearly to dissuade mortgagors from prepaying their mortgages. The reality is that a few trust companies stand to make enormous profits if they can discourage mortgagors from prepayment and thus carry their mortgages to full term. Look at it this way, some of the mortgages the trust companies hold have interest rates at more than double today's rates. I am not against anyone making a profit. But if they make that profit at the expense of the mortgagor, by changing the rules in the middle of the game, then I must stand against them, and I will try to assist the mortgagor.

October 20, 1983
Adjournment Debate
It is like playing with a double-headed coin. If you are a home owner with a 19.5 per cent mortgage, and a trust company can force you through the interest differential charge to keep your mortgage to full term, then the trust company is the winner.
If, however, you decide to prepay the mortgage and you agree to the interest differential charge demanded, the trust company is again the winner. Not only do they get the 19.5 per cent interest to full term of the mortgage but they demand an additional three month's interest penalty. Do you know of any parallel situation when you pay the full interest charged in a contract plus an additional three months' interest, plus other costs associated with the discharge of a debt?
The Minister, in her reply, said she was seeking a solution under the Canada Interest Act. Any action she may take under that statute may assist some home owner in the future but would not help those who are presently trapped.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should use the leverage she has with trust companies and require them to fulfil their verbal contractual agreements and adhere to the standard industry policy. They baited mortgagors to sign a multiple year mortgage on the understanding that they could prepay the mortgage upon the payment of three months' interest penalty, then they switched their policy.
Let me say that not all trust companies have used these devious plans to strip the home owner of his right to exercise an option that was standard in industry at the time the mortgage was written. Not all trust companies have engaged in this devious practice. But a handful of trust companies are holding at ransom 750,000 Canadians, and this should not happen.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Berger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-REFUSAL TO REWRITE MORTGAGES AT LOWER RATES. (B) PROTECTION REQUESTED FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred earlier to the clear understanding that has existed, or the tradition in the industry that home owners can prepay mortgages on the payment of three months' penalty. He asks the Minister to use the leverage she has. Unfortunately, while Members on all sides of the House sympathize with the predicament in which home owners may find themselves, a contract, as we all know, is a contract, and it is not for the Minister or any other Party to open a contract which has been signed between two parties. If there has been misrepresentation, however, this is a matter which a home owner can take up in a court of law. There are civil law remedies to settle disputes over contractual agreements. These cases of alleged oral misrepresentation have been referred to the Director of Investigation and Research under the Combines Investigations Act.
In this regard, the Director has examined and is still in the process of examining the complaints received within the Department on this subject. The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has always strongly supported and promoted full disclosure of all terms, conditions and obligations to borrowers.
The chief concern regarding those citizens unfortunate enough to be locked into high interest mortgages is that they may not have been fully aware of their current agreements. Unfortunately many did not realize that they had no legal right to prepay their mortgages prior to maturity with a maximum prepayment charge set at three months' interest. While a prepayment penalty of three months' interest has been a longstanding tradition, it is not rooted in law and lenders are under no statutory obligation to adhere to that practice.
However, officials in the Department have been asked to review the Canada Interest Act in order to determine means to ensure that borrowers in the future are fully informed of all rights and conditions at the time of signing.
In conclusion I would add that the allegations concerning oral misrepresentations are not solely against the Canada Trust Company. Other trust companies, life insurance companies, banks and investment firms have to date been implicated by complainants. These are the matters which are being looked into by the Director of Investigation and Research.

subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-DEVELOPMENT OF PREVENTIVE HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS. (B) HEALTH CARE FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question I asked of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on October 12. Before doing that, I remind the House of how we have repeatedly urged the Minister to stop playing politics with the health care needs of Canadians and to proceed without delay to the introduction of a new Canada Health Act which would reaffirm, clarify, strengthen and make enforceable the five basic principles of medicare from coast to coast, namely, universality, accessibility, portability, comprehensiveness and non-profit administration.
Such things as rising premiums, the spread of user fees to five out of ten Provinces, increasing levels of extra billing in certain areas of Canada and Government cutbacks are slowly but surely destroying medicare. We do not really know just when we will arrive at the point of no return. We do know that Conservative provincial Governments are definitely permitting new erosions of the principles of medicare.
Despite plenty of rhetoric from the Minister of National Health and Welfare about her concern for medicare, the Minister has still not put any concrete legislation before the House which would address these serious problems. She continues to dangle the idea of a new Canada Health Act before those Canadians who are concerned about medicare. And I have to admit she has been successful, at the political level at least, of appearing to be a great defender of medicare. However the moment of truth is near. For every day that goes by that we do not see a concrete proposal, cynicism grows among Canadians concerned about medicare as to whether or not the Minister is actually concerned about preserving medicare or whether the Liberal Party is concerned about preserving medicare not in itself but as an issue for the next election.
October 20, 1983

Unfortunately the Minister is also unwilling to address the very real need in our country for alternatives to the present health care model with which medicare must co-exist. The Minister has recognized that the greatest strides to be made in health care today are in the area of preventive medicine and health promotion. By improving the over-all health of the Canadian population we can reduce the need for Canada's current curative, doctor-dominated, high-tech and expensive health care system. Not only would Canadians be healthier but their health care system would be more cost-efficient, although in the final analysis that is not a good enough reason to do something. We want to do these things because they improve over-all health; that must be the real reason.
On October 12, I asked the Minister whether she intended to provide federal leadership in the development of such a health-oriented, broad-based and popular health care system for Canada. She resorted to the tired old cop-out that health was a provincial matter. Who is the Minister trying to kid? The federal Government has always played an important role in the evolution of medicare in this country. National medicare would not even be here today, sick as it is, if it were not for federal initiative. It would not be here at all if it were not for the initiative of the CCF-NDP in Saskatchewan, both in terms of hospital insurance and medicare. My constituents know that. They know the history of it, as do many Canadians. That is appropriate.
The Minister is at the very least being inconsistent. On the one hand she claims to be providing federal leadership by threatening sanctions against those Provinces which allow extra billing and impose user-fees. On the other hand, she claims she is constitutionally helpless when it comes to initiating the development of novel health care alternatives that would make Canada a healthier place in which to live, and which would take some of the pressure off the increasing costs that people are wrongly blaming on medicare when they should be blaming it on the health care model with which medicare has to co-exist.
The people of this country are sick and tired of political games such as the Minister is playing. They want the Minister to stop beating around the bush and to enact legislation that would address all the financial and structural problems plaguing medicare.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, Canadians must realize that in the final analysis health is not just related to a particular health care system, but to the social, economic and environmental dimension of our lives. The best principles of medicare imaginable, enforced to the limit, will not overcome the consequences of malnutrition caused by inner city poverty. They will not overcome exposure to hazards in the workplace. They will not overcome the fact of carcinogens in our food, water and environment. For in the final analysis, we are not just fighting for our health care system, but for that total health that will only come as we achieve greater social, economic and environmental justice.

The Hon. Member is anxious that we develop alternatives to the way in which health care services are currently delivered. However, he says we should forget the constitutional realities of this country.
Under our Constitution, each Province is responsible in its own right for determining the practice privileges of different types of health professionals, organizational arrangements with respect to their health services and payment arrangements. In this connection, it may be of interest to note that the federal Government from 1968 until 1977 recognized the costs of alternative payment arrangements for the insured services of medical practitioners for cost-sharing purposes under the Medical Care Act and these costs have been included in the base-year costs that are used for determining the amount of block funding under the current EPF arrangements.
It also may be of interest to you, Mr. Speaker, that under EPF, the federal Government does make a per capita grant yearly to each Province in respect of the extended health care services program.
